content: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic condition that significantly impacts quality of life and work productivity. Previous research has not provided definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of homeopathic treatments for IBS, and further high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been recommended to evaluate both the clinical and cost-effectiveness of these treatments. Two types of homeopathy were examined in this review: clinical homeopathy, where specific remedies are prescribed for specific conditions, and individualized homeopathy, where remedies are tailored to a person’s unique symptoms following a detailed consultation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of homeopathic treatments for IBS. To achieve this, databases such as MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, and others were searched for relevant studies up to August 31, 2018. The review included RCTs, cohort studies, and case-control studies that compared homeopathic treatments to placebo, other control treatments, or usual care in adults with IBS. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias and extracted data. The primary outcome was global improvement in IBS symptoms, measured using an IBS symptom severity score. Secondary outcomes included quality of life, abdominal pain, stool frequency, stool consistency, and adverse events. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE criteria, and the Cochrane risk of bias tool was employed to assess study quality. Statistical analyses included calculations of mean differences (MD) and risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Four RCTs involving 307 participants were included in the review. Two studies evaluated clinical homeopathy using remedies such as asafoetida or asafoetida combined with nux vomica for IBS with constipation (IBS-C). One study compared individualized homeopathy (consultation plus remedy) to usual care in female patients with IBS. Another study was a three-arm RCT comparing individualized homeopathy to supportive listening and usual care. The risk of bias was unclear in three studies (the two clinical homeopathy studies and the study comparing individualized homeopathy to usual care) and high for selective reporting in one clinical homeopathy study. The three-arm study comparing individualized homeopathy to supportive listening and usual care had a low risk of bias in four domains but a high risk of performance and detection bias. A meta-analysis of the two clinical homeopathy studies (171 participants with IBS-C) showed that, at two weeks, 73% of participants receiving asafoetida reported global symptom improvement compared to 45% in the placebo group (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.18; very low certainty evidence). In another study, 68% of participants receiving asafoetida plus nux vomica reported improvement compared to 52% in the placebo group (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.15; very low certainty evidence). In the study comparing individualized homeopathy to usual care (20 participants), the mean global improvement score at 12 weeks was 1.44 ± 4.55 in the homeopathy group versus 1.41 ± 1.97 in the usual care group (MD 0.03; 95% CI -3.16 to 3.22; very low certainty evidence). At six months, the mean IBS symptom severity score was 210.44 ± 112.4 in the homeopathy group compared to 237.3 ± 110.22 in the usual care group (MD -26.86, 95% CI -88.59 to 34.87; low certainty evidence). The mean quality of life score (EQ-5D) at six months was 69.07 in the homeopathy group compared to 63.41 in the usual care group (MD 5.66, 95% CI -4.69 to 16.01; low certainty evidence). In the study comparing individualized homeopathy to supportive listening, the mean IBS symptom severity score at six months was 210.44 ± 112.4 in the homeopathy group compared to 262 ± 120.72 in the supportive listening group (MD -51.56, 95% CI -129.94 to 26.82; very low certainty evidence). The mean quality of life score at six months was 69.07 in the homeopathy group compared to 63.09 in the supportive listening group (MD 5.98, 95% CI -8.13 to 20.09; very low certainty evidence). None of the included studies reported outcomes related to abdominal pain, stool frequency, stool consistency, or adverse events. The authors concluded that the evidence for the effectiveness and safety of homeopathy in treating IBS is highly uncertain. No definitive conclusions can be drawn, and further high-quality, adequately powered RCTs are needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of both clinical and individualized homeopathy for IBS compared to placebo or usual care.
